key_insight: Correcting hidden dataset biases substantially improves the true, out-of-distribution generalization of models that predict molecular binding affinity — reported gains come from fixing how data is split and evaluated rather than model changes.
problem_solved: Addresses over‑optimistic and unreliable binding affinity predictions caused by dataset biases (e.g., target/scaffold leakage and label distribution artifacts) that make reported performance not reflect real-world use.
method: Audit datasets to identify and quantify sources of bias (similarity/leakage between train and test, class/label imbalances).
Apply bias-mitigation strategies—realistic OOD train/test splits, reweighting or resampling, and controlled evaluation on held-out sets—and retrain models to measure true generalization improvements.
impact: Promotes more reliable ML models for drug discovery by shifting focus from tweaking architectures to fixing data curation and evaluation; encourages adoption of dataset-audit and OOD benchmarking best practices.
visual_elements: Before/after schematic of dataset splitting showing leakage eliminated (e.g., overlapping scaffolds removed).
Bar chart comparing model performance on biased vs corrected splits (apparent vs true generalization).
Similarity heatmap (train vs test) highlighting sources of leakage and their mitigation.
Checklist icon or flowchart of recommended dataset-audit and evaluation steps for practitioners.
paper_title: Addendum: Resolving data bias improves generalization in binding affinity prediction
paper_authors: David Graber, Peter Stockinger, Fabian Meyer, Siddhartha Mishra, Claus Horn
